Who assesses and bills property tax

Chicago sits inside Cook County, so county offices run the system for the city. The Cook County Assessor values the property, and the Cook County Treasurer bills and collects the tax. The Cook County Board of Review hears appeals once the Assessor has finished its pass.

  • Assessor's Office: sets estimated market values, mails reassessment notices and accepts first-level appeals when a township opens.
  • Board of Review: a separate appeal level with its own township calendar.
  • Treasurer's Office: sends the bills, takes payments and runs the delinquent tax sale. It is at 118 North Clark Street, Room 212, Chicago, IL 60602.

Most questions from a seller land with one of these three. Value questions go to the Assessor, appeal questions go to the Assessor first and then the Board of Review, and anything about a bill, a payment or a tax sale goes to the Treasurer. Calling the wrong office is the most common way to lose a few days before a closing.

On the Treasurer's website you can get a copy of a bill, search a property for delinquent taxes, see the taxing district debt attached to it and look for missing senior exemptions.

Chicago housing at a glance

Chicago had an estimated 2,731,585 residents in mid-2025 across 227.73 square miles on Lake Michigan. Owners live in 46.0% of occupied homes, so renters are the majority. The typical owner-occupied home is valued at $334,100 and median gross rent is $1,440.

Housing here is a patchwork. Brick bungalows from the early twentieth century run through large stretches of the residential map, mixed with two-flats, townhouses, condominiums and apartment buildings. A bungalow in one area and a condo near the Loop can carry bills that look unrelated. Residential values have moved from a median decrease of 7.7% in some areas to an increase of 131.8% in others, so the figure for your own street can sit far from any citywide number. Transit access also matters to value, with the L, Metra and Pace buses carrying about 1.3 million rides a day.

Installment due dates

Cook County dates move from year to year, and the Treasurer posts each one. Recent years show how much the calendar shifts:

  • Tax year 2024: first installment March 4, 2025 and second December 15, 2025.
  • Tax year 2023: first installment March 1, 2024 and second August 1, 2024.

Read the dates printed on your own bill, and check the Treasurer's due-dates page before you send a payment.

Exemptions appear as deductions on the second installment bill, which matters if you are a seller waiting on a credit. If a Certificate of Error for a valuation correction has been approved, refund timing comes from the Treasurer's Office.

How assessment appeals work

Cook County uses a two-level appeal system, and each level opens township by township. Chicago is divided into several townships, among them Rogers Park, Lakeview, Hyde Park, Lake, Jefferson, North Chicago and South Chicago, and the Assessor's calendar gives each one a last file date. Check the Assessor's site for your township's current window.

Cook County reassesses on a three-year cycle, rotating through the city, the north suburbs and the south and west suburbs. A property outside its turn can still be revalued after division work, permits or other special circumstances, and the owner would then receive a reassessment notice. The Board of Review runs its own township dates, listed in its Township and Exemption Dates document each year. Confirm your township's window there before you gather paperwork.

Whichever level you use, bring what shows your value is too high: a recent purchase price, an appraisal and sales of similar homes nearby.

What Chicago owners pay

The median Chicago homeowner bill rose 3.2% to $4,597 for tax year 2025. Overall Chicago taxes rose $196 million, or 2.2%, below the 3.1% rate of inflation for 2025, and homeowners picked up about three-fifths of that increase. Nearly 660,000 residential properties saw higher taxes, while fewer than 66,000 saw lower ones.

Countywide there were nearly 1.8 million bills for the 2025 tax year and a total levy above $19.9 billion. Commercial values in Chicago continued to decline, which shifts more of the load onto homes.

Exemptions soften the bill. The Homeowner Exemption reduces a home's equalized assessed value by $10,000. It applies to single-family homes, townhouses, condominiums, co-ops and buildings up to six units, and it renews automatically for properties that were not sold in the last year. A new owner must apply. The Treasurer's site also lists senior, senior freeze, disability and military exemptions.

Selling with unpaid taxes

The Treasurer holds a delinquent tax sale on December 15, 2026, and publishes brochures on how to avoid it in English, Spanish and Polish. Taxes from tax year 2023 are the ones on the lists of properties with delinquent taxes. Owners whose taxes have already gone to sale can use the Treasurer's If Taxes Were Sold page.

Search your PIN on the Treasurer's site to see whether any tax is delinquent. If a year is behind, ask the Treasurer and your title company for the payoff figure before closing, so the amount comes out of your proceeds and does not delay the sale.

A practical order of steps for a Chicago seller:

  • Search your PIN on the Treasurer's site and note any delinquent year.
  • Download a copy of the latest bill so the title company has the numbers.
  • Check whether your Homeowner Exemption is on the bill, since the buyer will need to apply for their own.
  • Ask the title company how the second installment will be credited at closing.

Since a buyer's lender will want clear title, a delinquent year can stall a sale. A cash buyer can close around an open balance, but you should still know the number first.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Chicago transfer tax

The City of Chicago's Real Property Transfer Tax is $5.25 per $500 of the transfer price, or fraction thereof. In general the buyer pays the larger share and the seller pays the supplemental portion for the Chicago Transit Authority.

Who generally owes the city transfer tax
PartyRate per $500 of priceWhat it covers
Buyer$3.75Base city portion
Seller$1.50Supplemental portion for the Chicago Transit Authority

Exempt transfers include those to or from a governmental body, deeds that secure debt, transfers under $500 and tax deeds. A refund of the CTA portion exists for buyers 65 or older who occupy the home for at least a year, when the price is $250,000 or less. The Tax Division is at 2 N. La Salle Street, Suite 1310. The Illinois state tax of 50 cents per $500 under 35 ILCS 200/31-10 is a separate tax.

Frequently asked questions

Who bills property tax in Chicago?

The Cook County Treasurer's Office. The Cook County Assessor sets the values, and the Board of Review hears appeals.

When are Chicago property tax installments due?

The dates change each year. Recent first installments fell between March 1 and March 4, and second installments came between August 1 and December 15. Check your bill.

What is the Cook County Homeowner Exemption?

A $10,000 reduction in a home's equalized assessed value for owner-occupied residences of up to six units. It appears on the second installment bill, and new owners must apply.

How much is the Chicago transfer tax?

$5.25 per $500 of transfer price. In general the buyer owes $3.75 and the seller $1.50.

Is there a Cook County tax sale in December 2026?

Yes. The Treasurer holds a delinquent tax sale on December 15, 2026 and publishes guides on avoiding it.

Peoria, IL Property Tax Guide: Offices, Dates and Selling With Tax Due

Cash Home Buyers in Illinois
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Peoria, IL Property Tax Guide: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Peoria, IL Property Tax Guide sale
  • Turn the Peoria, IL Property Tax Guide offer down and you owe us nothing

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Who sends the bill

The county does, not the city. A home within Peoria's limits gets one combined bill spanning the city, the schools and the rest of the taxing bodies on the parcel. The Peoria County Treasurer, who doubles as County Collector, mails it and takes the money. City Hall writes its own rules on registration and transfer tax but never mails a tax bill.

Taxes can be paid at the Treasurer, at participating banks or at township collectors, and the City of Peoria Township Collector is a separate office. Find out which one applies to your parcel before a check goes out.

Peoria housing at a glance

Peoria is the seat of Peoria County and the anchor of a metro area near 402,000 people. The city had an estimated 110,920 residents in July 2025, 2.0% below the 2020 count. Just 57.5% of homes are occupied by their owners, so landlords and tenants figure in many local sales. The median owner-occupied home is worth $156,200, and median rent is $1,005 a month.

Owner costs per month run $1,525 for a mortgage holder and $647 for someone without one. Hospitals drive the local economy, with the medical district clustered at Interstate 74 and Knoxville Avenue beside downtown. These are citywide figures, and individual streets can land far above or below them.

The 2026 assessment for City of Peoria Township

The county's notice for City of Peoria Township uses a January 1, 2026 valuation date. It sets 33.33% of market value as the target, reports a county median of 31.25%, and draws on sales from 2023 through 2025. One equalization factor, 1.0700, covers the residential, commercial, industrial and farm home site classes.

Owners who doubt a value should start with the township assessor at 427 W Main St, Peoria, IL 61606, (309) 324-7459. The Board of Review takes complaints from June 1 until 30 days after the changes are published, and a filed complaint is what preserves your right to appeal. This year's period closed September 30, so the next one begins June 1.

A quick self-check: divide your assessment by 33.33%. A result above what the house would fetch suggests it may be over-assessed.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Payment deadlines and late fees

One bill covers the year and splits into two halves, due in early June and early September. Payment or postmark one day after a due date or later brings 1.5% for every month or fraction of one, and there is no grace period.

Peoria payment checkpoints for 2025 taxes
CheckpointDetail
Bills mailedScheduled by May 1
Call if no billMay 15, 309-672-6065 option 5
InstallmentsEarly June and early September
Personal checks stopAfter mid-October
Collector's last day before saleEarly November, 5 p.m.

The sale follows that last day. Sold taxes can still be redeemed afterward at the County Clerk, with the buyer's interest and fees.

City rules that touch a house sale

Peoria's transfer tax is $2.50 for each $1,000 of value or fraction of $1,000 stated on the transfer declaration, under a 1989 ordinance. It is paid at the Peoria County recording office. If money changes hands on a commercial or multi-family property, the city also wants a zoning certificate dated within the past year, issued by Community Development at 419 Fulton, Room 300, (309) 494-8600.

The city runs a property registration program. A home must be registered if it is any of the following:

  • rented to a tenant, including a family member
  • vacant for six months or longer
  • an investment property, meaning not the deeded owner's residence
  • being sold on contract for deed until the deed transfers
  • a multi-family building
  • a short-term rental of 29 days or less
  • in foreclosure

Registration fees are waived for a few cases, including a vacant house listed for sale and a house in probate, though those still have to register. Past fees were $75 for a single-family home, $75 plus $20 per added unit for multi-family, $75 per short-term rental unit with an 8% room tax, and $300 per parcel every six months for foreclosure. Confirm the current amounts with the Office of Accounts Receivable at 419 Fulton Street, Room 100.

Selling with taxes owed

Peoria County sells unpaid taxes in early November. Buyers bid from 0% to 9% interest, and if nobody bids the county takes the parcel at 9% as trustee. Interest is added at the sale and every six months. The owner still holds title during redemption, which defaults to two years and can be stretched to three. For homes of one to six units the minimum is two and a half years.

Redemption goes to the Peoria County Clerk, 324 Main St, Room 101, in one payment of cash, a cashier's check or a money order. Title company and personal checks are not accepted. A seller in that position should order the Clerk's redemption estimate and share it with the closer, since a lender will not close over an unredeemed sale.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Before you list a Peoria house

Sort out three things first. Find out whether the house falls under the city's registration program, since a rental, a vacant house or a house in probate has to be registered even when the fee is waived. Ask the Treasurer for the current-year bill status and the Clerk whether any year was sold. If the property is commercial or multi-family, request the zoning certificate early so it does not hold up the deed.

At closing the title company will want the registration status, the transfer declaration and a payoff for any sold taxes. A cash buyer skips the lender's review, but the county records and the city transfer tax still apply, so the paperwork list does not get shorter.

Homestead and other exemptions

The county lists an owner-occupied exemption of $6,000 off equalized assessed value, a senior exemption of $5,000, a returning service member exemption of $5,000 and a disabled persons exemption of $2,000. Disabled service members receive $2,500, $5,000 or a full exemption depending on the service-connected rating. The senior deferral program charges 3% and is repaid when the home is sold, so a seller who used it should expect a payoff at closing. Questions go to the Supervisor of Assessments at 309-672-6910.

Frequently asked questions

Does the City of Peoria collect my property tax?

No. The Peoria County Treasurer sends and collects the bill, and taxes can also be paid at participating banks or at the township collector. The city handles registration of rentals, vacant and foreclosure properties and its own transfer tax.

What is the Peoria transfer tax rate?

$2.50 for each $1,000 of value or fraction of $1,000 stated on the transfer declaration. It is paid at the Peoria County recording office, and commercial or multi-family transfers need a current zoning certificate.

Does a vacant Peoria house need city registration?

Yes, once it has sat empty six months or more. A vacant house on the market gets a fee waiver but still has to be registered, with proof of the listing, and a house in probate is treated the same way. The Office of Accounts Receivable at City Hall handles it.

When is the Peoria appeal deadline for assessments?

Complaints run from June 1 until 30 days after the township publishes changes. Talk to the City of Peoria Township assessor first.

How late can Peoria taxes be paid before the sale?

The Treasurer must receive payment by 5 p.m. on the last day in early November, and postmarks do not count. After a sale, taxes are redeemed through the County Clerk instead.

Cash Home Buyers in Illinois
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Rockford, IL Property Tax Guide: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Rockford, IL Property Tax Guide sale
  • Turn the Rockford, IL Property Tax Guide offer down and you owe us nothing

Owe Rockford Property Tax? Get a Cash Offer

We buy Rockford houses as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Behind on Rockford property tax?
We buy Rockford houses as-is, and the title company pays unpaid tax from the proceeds.
Get My Cash Offer →

County offices behind a Rockford bill

Two Winnebago County offices do the work: the Treasurer mails and collects the bill, and the Supervisor of Assessments produces the values it is built on. Both sit in the County Administration Building at 404 Elm Street in Rockford. A sliver of the city reaches into Ogle County, and parcels there are billed from Ogle.

  • Treasurer, Room 205, weekdays 8 to 5, phone (815) 319-4400: bills, payments, and the yearly tax sale.
  • Supervisor of Assessments, Room 301, same weekday hours, phone (815) 319-4460: change notices, homestead exemptions, and the Board of Review.
  • County Clerk, Room 101, phone (815) 319-4253: sold taxes and the extension of rates.

One Rockford statement lists many taxing bodies: the county, the city, the park district, the library, the airport authority, Rockford Public Schools District 205 and Community College 511. What you owe turns on the tax code printed on your bill.

Due dates and penalties

Bills go into the mail in early May. For 2025 taxes, installments fell on June 12 and September 11, 2026, and the treasurer charges 1.5% for each month an installment stays unpaid. Partial payments are refused.

For owners with no older delinquent years, Friday, December 4, 2026 is the final day to pay before the unpaid tax goes to sale. The office wants payment in hand or made online that day, and it will not honor a postmark on the last day.

  • E-check through the website costs nothing.
  • Cards add 2.25%, which the payment servicer keeps.
  • A bounced check costs $35, and title or mortgage companies lacking the original bill pay $3 per parcel for a duplicate.

Anything owed for 2024 or earlier cannot be paid on the treasurer's site. A tax buyer has normally covered those years already, so the County Clerk handles them.

Which rate applies to my Rockford parcel?

The county's rate report for tax year 2024 totals 9.4764 for tax code 001, the code for parcels inside the city limits and Rockford School District 205. A parcel that pairs the Rockford Park District with Harlem School District 122 and a different library falls in another code, and that code totals 8.3297.

The clerk's extension office works out these rates every year and links to the state's Tax Rate Finder. A parcel inside the East Side TIF district shows a TIF line on its bill, and the growth in tax there is spent on projects within that district.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to contest a Rockford value

Call the township assessor first. If that fails, file a complaint with the Winnebago County Board of Review inside the 30 calendar days that follow publication of your township's assessments. The Board describes four levels: the township assessor, the Board itself, the state Property Tax Appeal Board, then court.

The 2026 cycle for Rockford Township ran like this, and the same order repeats each year:

  • Values went online July 31 at 5:00 p.m., and notices were mailed August 3.
  • Publication came August 5, and complaints closed September 4.
  • Added evidence was due September 29 for cuts under $100,000 and October 14 for bigger requests.

Cherry Valley, Durand, Laona and Owen townships follow the same dates, while Harlem and Roscoe run a day behind. The Board suggests looking at its page in mid-July for the next set. Anyone unhappy with the Board's ruling has 30 days from the decision, by postmark, to take the case to the state appeal board.

Relief for older owners

Winnebago County describes three senior programs. They sit on top of the general homestead exemption that any owner-occupant should see on the bill.

  • Senior Citizen Exemption: owners who are 65 or older in the assessment year and live in the home on January 1 get $5,000 off the equalized assessed value. File by December 31 of that year.
  • Assessment Freeze: locks the equalized assessed value while the owner remains eligible, with a $65,000 income ceiling. Apply before July 1.
  • Tax Deferral: open at 65 and older with household income up to $75,000. The state advances the deferred tax, to a limit of $7,500 a year, and the owner repays with interest. Apply by March 1.

Sellers should note the repayment rule: a deferral comes due when the property sells or the estate settles. The Supervisor of Assessments also warns that online claims of a nationwide freeze or an October 15 federal filing date are false.

What a tax sale does to an unpaid bill

The county puts the debt up for bid, not the house. Registered buyers bid interest rates at a live auction, with a cap of 9%, and the lowest bid wins. That buyer pays the county, and the owner then redeems through the County Clerk.

The redemption window is 2.5 years for most homes under 35 ILCS 200/21-350, and some county pages say three. Vacant non-farm land, buildings with seven or more units, and commercial or industrial property get one year. The buyer may extend, and interest climbs as time passes, so call the clerk for the real deadline and payoff before you plan a sale around it. Pay with cash, a money order or a cashier's check for the exact sum.

If nobody redeems, the buyer can ask the court for a tax deed. Your closing agent can explain how a sold tax is handled at the table once you hold the clerk's figure.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Rockford housing and local conditions

Rockford is the fifth-largest city in Illinois, about 90 miles west-northwest of downtown Chicago on the Rock River. It had an estimated 147,384 residents in July 2025, down from 148,655 in 2020, and 61,324 households with a median household income of $54,752.

Housing is where Rockford differs most from the Chicago suburbs. Owner-occupied homes have a median value of $129,000, owners occupy only 54.9% of housing, and median gross rent is $985. Neighborhoods on the near east side were hit by Keith Creek flooding in 2006 and 2007, and a July 2024 flood overwhelmed the city's stormwater systems. Roofs and drainage are worth documenting for buyers.

Rental registration before a sale

Every residential rental inside city limits belongs on the City of Rockford's registry, which short-term rentals also use. The registry grew out of the Residential Quality Support Ordinance, it costs nothing to use, and skipping it can bring fines of $50 to $750 per day for each property.

Registration asks for the property address, number of dwelling units, and contact details for the owner, manager and tenant. Registered owners get emails when police or fire respond to the property and before a code enforcement inspection.

If tenants live in the house you plan to sell, check that its registration is current before you list.

Steps for the tax bill at closing

Get a payoff figure for your parcel number from the treasurer, ask the County Clerk whether any year was sold, and pass both numbers to the title company handling the closing.

  • Find the 2025 bill and the parcel number.
  • Check that the exemptions on the bill are yours, since a senior deferral or freeze changes the payoff.
  • Ask the clerk about 2024 and earlier years if a bill looks unpaid.
  • Look at your rental registry status if tenants have lived there.

When repairs or old taxes make a listing hard, a cash buyer who takes the house as it stands is another option, and a cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay Rockford property tax?

Pay the Winnebago County Treasurer at 404 Elm Street, Room 205, on the county website, or by phone. E-checks cost nothing, and cards carry 2.25%. Many area banks and credit unions also accept payments if you bring the bill.

How much is the late penalty on a Rockford tax bill?

It is 1.5% per month on each late installment. The office adds that penalties change every 30 days and partial payments are refused, so use the online payment page for a figure that includes the penalty.

When can I appeal my Rockford assessment?

Within 30 calendar days after your township's assessments are published, usually late July or early August. A call to the township assessor before then can sometimes fix a mistake informally.

Is Rockford in Winnebago County or Ogle County?

Mostly Winnebago County, where Rockford is the seat of government, but a portion of the city extends into Ogle County. Parcels in that Ogle portion are billed by Ogle County, so read the county named on your bill.

Is it possible to sell a Rockford house that owes back taxes?

Yes. The title company can pay the tax out of the sale proceeds at the closing. If a tax buyer already holds the tax, call the Winnebago County Clerk at (815) 319-4253 for a redemption figure, payable in certified funds or cash.

Who bills property tax in the city of Champaign

Champaign does not mail a city tax bill. Each parcel in town is billed by the Champaign County Treasurer (also the Collector), and that single bill covers the schools and every other district that overlaps the property. The Champaign County Supervisor of Assessments handles valuation, and because the city matches Champaign City township, one township assessor covers all of it.

Selling is simpler for it. A single PIN identifies the parcel, and two county offices answer your questions, wherever the house sits.

The Champaign market in brief

Champaign is a city of about 23 square miles in central Illinois. Population was estimated at 91,195 in mid-2025, with 43.8% of homes lived in by owners, which leaves renters as the larger group. The typical owner-occupied home is valued at $210,900, and median gross rent is $1,123. The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign on the east side and Parkland College on the northwest give the market a large student population during the school year.

A landlord selling a rental near campus will often be dealing with tenants and a lease cycle, and the tax bill follows the parcel no matter who lives in it. Older houses, especially those built in the 1980s or earlier, draw close looks at the roof and heating system, so check both before you list.

Demand shifts from one pocket of the city to the next:

  • Downtown Champaign: the historic core with newer mixed-use buildings and a parking deck.
  • Campustown: the Green Street district beside the university, where high-rise student apartments have opened since 2008.
  • North Prospect: a shopping corridor on the city's northern edge.
  • Northwest and west sides: home to Parkland College and St. Thomas More High School.

Due dates and how to pay

Expect your bill in the mail by early May. Half is normally due in June and half in September, and a postmark on the due date counts. The coupon shows the exact dates.

Interest of 1.5% a month builds on late payments. Personal checks are taken through September 30, and a returned payment is void with a $30 charge plus statutory interest.

  • Online or by phone at 217-834-8713, with a card or eCheck. The processing vendor charges a fee.
  • In person at the Treasurer's counter, 102 E. Main Street in Urbana.

Keep the payment confirmation or canceled check. At closing the title company may ask to see proof that the year's installments are paid.

How to challenge an assessment

Complaints go to the Board of Review between July 1 and September 10. The office is open 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., Monday through Thursday, and sees people by appointment too. Township assessors value a house on January 1 at one-third of market value, and owners get a change notice from the Supervisor of Assessments ahead of the window.

Collect proof that fits your property: the price you paid if the purchase was recent, an appraisal, and sales of comparable homes nearby. After September 10 the board reviews the complaints and issues written decisions.

Before you file, look at the change notice you received and compare your value with recent sales on your block. If your value is in line with what similar houses sold for, a complaint is unlikely to change anything. If it is higher, a clean set of comparables and your closing statement are the strongest things you can bring. Call the Board of Review during its Monday to Thursday hours if you want to ask how to submit the paperwork.

Homestead exemptions

Every reduction here is taken from equalized assessed value ahead of the tax rate.

For forms, call the Assessment Office at 217-384-3760. Faxed or emailed applications are refused. If you moved in recently, ask whether an earlier owner's exemption carried over before assuming it did.

Getting the tax side ready before you list

A little groundwork saves trouble at the closing table. Pull your PIN and write down which installments you have paid this year. Look at your last bill for any exemption that is currently applied, and call the Assessment Office at 217-384-3760 if you are unsure, since the buyer will need to apply for their own. Check the change notice for your assessed value too, because a buyer's agent may ask about it.

If the house is a rental, tell the Treasurer where bills should go after the sale. Tenants who pay a share of the tax through rent should hear about the new mailing arrangement from you rather than from a collection notice.

If property tax goes unpaid

Tax still open after 4:30 p.m. on October 29 is sold to an investor at the county's October 30 sale. Your house is not what gets sold. Afterward you owe the amount sold plus interest and redeem through the County Clerk.

The Clerk mails a Take Notice inside four months of the sale. Redemption usually runs 3 years from the sale date, with exceptions listed in 35 ILCS 200/21-350. Miss it, and the investor can ask the circuit court for a deed.

Selling a Champaign house when tax is still due

Start with the PIN. The Treasurer can tell you which installments are paid, and your title company or attorney can say whether tax is owed for the year. Depending on the closing and recording dates, a bill may be addressed to the previous owner, who has to forward it to the new owner.

With open installments, ask the title company how they will be settled at closing. An early number lets you pick a closing date with room to spare. For a rental, put the tenants' lease end date on the same checklist.

A rough order of steps: pull the PIN, call the Treasurer for the payment status, confirm what the title company will pay from your proceeds, and make sure the buyer's mailing address goes to the Treasurer so the next bill reaches the right person. A cash buyer can usually close around an open installment, and you do not need to repair the house to the standard a lender's appraiser would expect.

  • Assessment Office, exemptions and forms: 217-384-3760.
  • County Clerk, redemption after a tax sale: 217-384-3722.
  • Treasurer's card and eCheck line: 217-834-8713.

Frequently asked questions

Does the city of Champaign collect its own property tax?

No. Bills come from the Champaign County Treasurer, who collects the money for every parcel in the city and passes it on to the districts.

When is Champaign property tax due?

The bill arrives by early May, and the two installments usually fall in June and September. Your coupon lists the dates.

When can I file an assessment complaint for a Champaign home?

From July 1 to September 10, filed with the Champaign County Board of Review. Its office keeps 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. hours, Monday through Thursday.

What is the senior exemption in Champaign?

It takes $5,000 off equalized assessed value if you turn 65 by the end of the assessment year. A separate assessment freeze exists for household income up to $75,000.

Naperville at a glance

Naperville is a Chicago suburb that sits in two counties and six townships. In DuPage County it takes in parts of Winfield, Milton, Naperville and Lisle townships, and in Will County parts of Wheatland and DuPage townships. The city had 149,540 residents in 2020 and an estimated 153,114 by July 2025.

Owners live in 74.8% of homes, and the middle value of an owned home is $540,200. At that price level each installment is a large check, so a seller is better off settling the bill cleanly before closing.

Which office sends your bill

A township assessor values each parcel, and the county that holds it does the billing. In DuPage County, the Treasurer at 421 N. County Farm Road in Wheaton mails one bill a year with two coupons attached. A slice of the city is in Will County, so the issuer printed on your own bill tells you which office to call.

The city levies its own share as well. That money mostly covers long-term obligations such as public safety, IMRF pensions and debt service, and it is the chief support for the Naperville Public Library and Naper Settlement. Sales, income, transfer and utility taxes plus service charges carry the rest. The levy draws on equalized value from the five townships that contain the city.

Due dates and penalties

Bills for 2025 went out April 29, 2026. Installments fall every year in early June and early September, and a new calendar with new dates is published each year.

  • Late payments owe 1 1/2% interest per month, judged by the U.S. postmark and never a meter mark.
  • Returned checks cost $25.
  • Double payments often happen when a title company and a mortgage servicer both pay. Only the person who made the extra payment can claim the refund, by notarized affidavit.

Before closing, ask the title company to confirm which installments are paid and who is sending the next one, so nobody pays twice.

How to appeal a Naperville Township value

Start with the informal Assessor Review at the Naperville Township Assessor. A formal appeal must be filed within 30 days of publication of the assessment list. The cycle repeats each fall, and neighboring townships inside the city publish on their own schedules, so phone your township assessor or check the DuPage assessment status page for the current dates.

  • Only assessed value can be challenged. A high tax bill by itself is no grounds.
  • Filing is electronic, through the county's SmartFile e-filing system.
  • DuPage wants three or more comparables, and for a market value case they should be recent sales.
  • Assessed values rest on the three prior years of sales, with later sales weighted more.

Written Board of Review decisions follow the end of all county hearings, typically the next March. Further review lies with the state appeal board or the courts.

Exemptions on a Naperville bill

These are the common ones on a DuPage bill:

  • The residential exemption, called the general homestead exemption in statute, for owners living in the house by the first of January. The cap is $8,000 where a county adjoins one with 3,000,000 or more residents, as DuPage does (35 ILCS 200/15-175).
  • The senior citizens homestead exemption, for owners who turned 65 during the tax year and can show age and ownership.
  • The senior assessment freeze, which carries a $65,000 household income ceiling.
  • A $2,000 reduction for disabled persons, plus exemptions for disabled and returning service members.
  • A homestead improvement exemption shielding up to $25,000 of added assessment, continuing up to four years.

Residential and improvement exemptions start at the township assessor. Senior and veteran applications can go to the Supervisor of Assessments, 630-407-5858. If you just bought, tell the township office early so the exemption lands on the next bill.

City transfer tax on a sale

Under city ordinance, the buyer of residential or commercial property in incorporated Naperville purchases a transfer tax stamp priced at $1.50 for each $500 of the sale price, with the price rounded up to the next $500. A deed change without a sale, such as a trust transfer, divorce or refinance, needs a free exempt stamp.

Bring three things: a Statement of Open Account requested no later than seven business days ahead of closing, a signed contract or the state transfer declaration, and the deed that will be recorded. Allow up to seven business days for processing. An address outside the city owes no city stamp, and the city's Your Place tool shows whether a house is inside.

Selling with taxes owed

Balances still open after the last payment day go to the DuPage sale in mid-November. Bidders compete by lowering an interest rate from 9% toward 0%, and the winning rate applies right away and every six months after. The County Clerk then runs redemption.

  • Residences of one to six units get at least 2 1/2 years to redeem and other property at least 2, and the buyer may stretch either to 3 (35 ILCS 200/21-350).
  • Before the sale the Treasurer adds a $10 publication and certified mailing charge, and $104 in sale costs.
  • Redeeming adds a $50 Clerk fee, the buyer's notice costs and any tax deed legal costs.

The tax buyer may also pay the next year's bill and add it to the redemption total with a 12% yearly penalty. If your parcel was sold, request a redemption figure from the Clerk before listing. A buyer's lender will want the redemption cleared before closing, and a cash sale that skips the lender still has to deal with the Clerk.

Floods, schools and access when you list

Buyers ask about schools first. District 203 serves central and northern Naperville through Naperville Central and Naperville North high schools. Indian Prairie District 204 covers the west and southwest, with Neuqua Valley, Metea Valley and Waubonsie Valley. The Will County pieces of the city also reach into the Plainfield and Valley View districts.

I-88 crosses the north end, US 34 and Illinois Route 59 run through town, and Metra and Amtrak serve the BNSF line. The city has seen two major floods, in 1996 and 2013, and parts of it drain to the DuPage River's West Branch, so expect drainage questions from buyers.

Frequently asked questions

Which county sends my Naperville bill?

Most parcels get a DuPage County Treasurer bill, though part of the city lies in Will County. The bill names its issuer, and the township assessor can confirm your township.

How is the Naperville transfer stamp priced?

At $1.50 per $500 of price, rounded up to the next $500, and the buyer buys the stamp. Request the Statement of Open Account at least seven business days before closing.

Can a Naperville owner appeal the tax amount itself?

No. An appeal targets assessed value, and a high bill has no bearing on valuation, so bring sales or comparable evidence.

How long do I have to file a Naperville Township appeal?

A formal appeal must be filed within 30 days of publication of the list, and an informal Assessor Review comes first. The dates shift each fall, so check with the assessor.

How long does redemption last after a sale?

At least 2 1/2 years for a one-to-six unit residence, extendable by the buyer to 3 years. The DuPage County Clerk handles it.

Who bills property tax on a Bloomington house

The bill comes from McLean County, not the city. Bloomington is the county seat, and one office, the treasurer and tax collector, mails a single bill for each of about 68,000 parcels, collecting for nearly 200 taxing districts. Find it at the Government Center, 115 E. Washington Street, Room M101, or call (309) 888-5180.

Valuing the property is handled elsewhere. Inside the city, the City of Bloomington Township assessor sets values. Equalization and exemptions belong to the Supervisor of Assessments, the chief county assessment officer, at (309) 888-5130, and complaints go to the Board of Review. City hall sends no property tax bill, although it registers rental buildings and collects its own local taxes.

  • Treasurer: payments, duplicate bills, delinquent tax and the yearly tax sale.
  • Assessors: values, property record cards, exemptions and mailing address updates.
  • Board of Review: assessment complaints, at (309) 888-5132.

Bloomington housing market

An estimated 78,804 people lived here in 2025, a 0.1% rise from 78,680 in 2020. Homeowners occupy 61.9% of occupied homes and the rest, roughly 38 in 100, are rentals, a fact worth knowing if an investor may buy your house. The typical owned home is valued at $203,300, with median rent of $1,050 a month.

Normal is Bloomington's neighbor. Bloomington District 87 and McLean County Unit District 5 teach most students in the city, with small portions in Olympia District 16. The district name on your bill shows which applies to you.

Due dates and penalties

Installments fall due in the first week of June and the first week of September, with all dates subject to change. Under 35 ILCS 200/20-15, a bill that never showed up does not erase the tax. No bill by mid-May? Ask the treasurer for a duplicate.

Typical McLean County collection calendar

Interest on a late payment is 1.5% a month, beginning the day after the due date. Postmark by the due date and you are on time.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to pay

The office will not take partial payments, and it sends no receipt unless you request one. Your canceled check or bank statement is proof enough.

  • By mail to the lockbox: McLean County Collector, P.O. Box 843637, Kansas City, MO 64184-3637.
  • In person, Monday to Friday from 8:00 to 4:30, at the Washington Street address above.
  • Drop boxes stay open day and night, by the Washington Street side of the lot or the East Street entrance.
  • Online or by phone with a credit card (a convenience fee applies), or by annual automatic withdrawal.
  • At a participating local bank.

Once the October personal check cutoff passes, only certified funds work, and the office takes nothing on sale day. State law charges a mortgage company $5.00 for a duplicate bill. After a refinance or payoff, send the Supervisor of Assessments a change of address so bills find you.

How to appeal your assessment

The Board of Review accepts a complaint for 30 days after the township's notice runs in the newspaper, and that notice gives your township's equalization factor. Bloomington Township is a different township in the same county with its own notice and factor, so find out which one holds your parcel before relying on a deadline or a number.

Assessments draw on the three years of market value before January 1 of the assessment year, then an equalization factor moves the result to 33.33%. Nothing late gets heard. Nonfarm owners file form PTAX-230, and the Board sits inside the Government Center in the Supervisor of Assessments' office.

A state disaster declaration after severe storms lets owners of damaged homes apply for reassessment on form PTAX-245. If yours took damage, ask the assessor whether that process is open now.

Homestead exemptions

An exemption trims taxable value ahead of the rate, so what you save follows your tax rate. Only your primary residence counts.

  • General homestead: up to $6,000, first filed with the county assessment office.
  • Homestead improvement: up to $75,000 of market value, or $25,000 assessed, usually granted automatically for four years.
  • Senior citizens: $5,000, with an initial PTAX-324 and proof of age.
  • Low-income senior freeze: household income under $75,000, using PTAX-340, which the county mails each year around February 1 to current senior exemption holders.
  • Disabled persons: $2,000, renewed each year by December 31.
  • Returning service members: $5,000 for the year of return and the following year.
  • Disabled service members: $2,500, $5,000 or up to $250,000, depending on the rating.

Seniors can ask the treasurer about deferral at (309) 888-5180. Buyers file their own claims once the sale closes.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Rental registration in Bloomington

Rental owners inside the city limits register every year through the city's Rental Property Program. Cost is $65 a building, with $5 more per unit once a building has three or more, and each registration lasts through December 31.

New owners cannot inherit a registration, so a buyer files again. Renting or occupying a covered building also requires a Certificate of Inspection. If a building is rated "fair," the city may ask for a $5,000 letter of credit or pledged account until it passes. Follow-up inspections run $100 per appointment and a missed one costs $75. Clear open violations before listing, because they feed a buyer's repair requests.

Selling and the tax bill

Illinois bills tax after the fact, so a house sold during the year still has bills to come. The seller usually gives the buyer a credit at closing for the share built up, and the buyer pays the next bill. Get the title company to show in writing how the credit was figured, and verify the parcel's payment status before you sign. If a prior installment was missed, the unpaid bill stays attached to the parcel, which is why the check matters.

Before you list, pull your latest bill, your exemption confirmations and any rental registration paperwork into one folder. A buyer and the title company will ask for each of them.

If you pay through a mortgage escrow, confirm shortly before each due date that the lender has paid. After a payoff, update your mailing address with the Supervisor of Assessments so notices reach you.

Frequently asked questions

Which office do I call about a Bloomington property tax bill?

Call the McLean County treasurer at (309) 888-5180 for payments and duplicate bills, and the county assessor at (309) 888-5130 for values, exemptions and mailing addresses. The city of Bloomington does not send the bill.

When is the second installment of Bloomington property tax due?

In the first week of September each year. Interest of 1.5% per month starts the day after the due date.

How long do I have to appeal a Bloomington assessment?

You get 30 days from the newspaper notice for your township, and a late complaint is not heard. Look for the notice every year.

Does Bloomington require rental registration when I sell?

Registration belongs to the owner, and the city says it cannot transfer to a new owner. A buyer of a rental registers anew and pays the printed fee of $65 per building.

Can I pay McLean County tax with a card?

Yes, online or by phone, with a convenience fee. The office also accepts mail, in-person payments, a 24-hour drop box, local banks and annual automatic withdrawal.

Who sends the bill

Cook County, not the City of Evanston, runs the property tax system. Values come from the Cook County Assessor's Office, appeals beyond that go to the Cook County Board of Review, and the Cook County Treasurer mails bills and collects payment. Evanston is its own assessment township, so when the Assessor reassesses, your parcel is grouped with other Evanston parcels.

The city does collect charges tied to a sale: the local real estate transfer tax and the final water bill, both covered below. Evanston property also sits in Evanston-Skokie School District 65 for grades through 8 and Evanston Township High School District 202 for high school. Those two districts are among the taxing bodies listed on your bill.

Installment due dates and how to pay

For tax year 2025 the first installment was due April 1, 2026 and the second October 1, 2026. Dates change from year to year, so go by the ones printed on your own bill. The second-installment mailing that year ran about two months late because of a technology overhaul of the county's tax system, and owners could look up bills online before the paper copies arrived.

Illinois law sets a firm rule for mailed checks: a payment counts as made on the date of a United States Postal Service postmark, while FedEx or UPS deliveries count on the day they arrive. A mailed payment can come back unprocessed if it lacks the PIN or the original coupon. In person, the Treasurer accepts payment at nearly 400 Chase Bank locations in Illinois and some community banks. Delinquent bills go to the Treasurer's office at 118 North Clark Street in Chicago.

How the Assessor values an Evanston home

Single-family homes, condos and small apartment buildings are Class 2, assessed at 10% of estimated market value. Cook County reassesses each township once every three years. During the last Evanston reassessment, notices were mailed in April 2025 and owners had until May 21, 2025 to appeal.

The Assessor's figures for Evanston Township show how its estimates compare with actual sales:

  • Single-family homes: $675,000 median sale price in 2024, $636,000 Assessor estimate for 2025
  • Condos: $294,000 median sale price in 2024, $265,000 estimate for 2025
  • Small apartment buildings: $620,000 median sale price in 2024, $592,000 estimate for 2025

The amount actually taxed is the equalized assessed value: the assessed value times a yearly equalizer the Illinois Department of Revenue sets for all of Cook County. Exemptions come off that number. The Homeowner Exemption subtracts $10,000 and the Senior Exemption subtracts $8,000, and both currently renew automatically.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to appeal your assessment

Start with the Assessor, then go to the Board of Review if you need to. Each accepts filings only while Evanston Township is open for appeals, and the windows are set on the Assessor's calendar in the year Evanston comes up. Assessor appeals are filed online, cost nothing and don't require an attorney.

The Assessor recognizes three grounds:

  • Lack of uniformity, where similar nearby homes carry lower assessments
  • Overvaluation, backed by a recent closing statement or the purchase prices of comparable homes
  • Incorrect description, such as the wrong square footage on your notice

The office gives a rule of thumb. When the listed characteristics are right and its estimate lands within 10% of what you think the home is worth, an appeal probably won't move the bill much. It also doesn't set a home's value equal to one recent sale.

A reduction that's granted holds until the next reassessment if nothing about the property changes. If you missed a window, appeal when the township next opens. A Certificate of Error, once approved, corrects a valuation after the fact, and the Treasurer handles any refund.

Evanston transfer tax

Evanston has had its own real estate transfer tax since 1986, under Ordinance 33-O-86. The seller typically pays unless the contract says otherwise, and the money goes to the General Fund. State transfer stamps add a separate charge of 50 cents for each $500 of value or fraction, under 35 ILCS 200/31-15.

Exempt transactions pay a $100 stamp fee under Evanston City Code 3-25-8-1. The city issues its transfer stamps electronically under Ordinance 18-O-25.

Getting the transfer stamp before closing

Request the stamp through the city's online service request portal or by calling the 3-1-1 center at 847-448-4311. The city doesn't take in-person applications.

  • Send the request 7 to 10 business days before closing.
  • Processing takes 5 business days, counted from the business day after the city receives your request.
  • There is no expedited handling and no exceptions.
  • Upload the signed Evanston Real Estate Declaration Form, plus the sale contract or deed, to the service request.

A stamp is released only after the documents check out and every debt owed to the city is paid. The final water bill is generated along with the request, except for condos and vacant land, and you pay it through the city's water billing site. Payment works online, in person at the City Collector's Office at 909 Davis Street, or by mail. Stamps of $5,000 to $49,999 need a credit card, cashier's check, title company check or wire. At $50,000 or more, the city requires a cashier's check or wire.

Evanston housing snapshot

Evanston sits on Lake Michigan about 12 miles north of the Loop, bordered by Chicago, Skokie and Wilmette. Population is 76,380 across 31,705 households. The median owner-occupied home is valued at $481,200, owners live in 56.2% of housing units, and median household income is $96,434. Median rent is $1,762. The CTA Purple Line and Metra's Union Pacific North line serve the city, with Metra stops at Main Street, Davis Street and Central Street.

Property tax at an Evanston closing

Cook County bills in two installments for a tax year that has already ended, so a sale almost always lands in the middle of a bill. The sale contract and the title company decide how the current bills are split between seller and buyer.

Before you list, look at which exemptions appear on the current bill. The Treasurer's website has tools to see how a bill changed, view taxing district debt and search for missing senior exemptions. If you're behind on tax, get the payoff balance from the Treasurer so the title company can clear it at closing. A cash buyer still goes through the same transfer stamp and water bill steps, so start the city request early.

Frequently asked questions

Who sends the property tax bill for an Evanston house?

The Cook County Treasurer sends it, not the City of Evanston. Bills go out in two installments, and tax year 2025 installments were due April 1 and October 1, 2026. The County Assessor sets the value the bill rests on.

How much is Evanston's real estate transfer tax?

It's $5 per $1,000 of value on sales up to $1,500,000, $7 on the slice from $1,500,000.01 to $5,000,000 and $9 above that. The seller usually pays unless the contract says otherwise, and a $100 fee applies to exempt transfers.

How long does an Evanston transfer stamp take?

Plan on 5 business days after the city receives your request, and submit it 7 to 10 business days before closing. There's no expedited service, and requests are accepted only online or through 3-1-1.

When can I appeal my Evanston assessment?

Only while the Assessor has Evanston Township open, which happens when the township is reassessed, about every three years. If you miss it, appeal the next time the township opens.

What percent of market value is an Evanston home assessed at?

Class 2 residential property in Cook County is assessed at 10% of estimated market value. Tax is then based on the equalized assessed value, which multiplies by the state equalizer and subtracts exemptions such as the $10,000 Homeowner Exemption.
